description:
Fiddle Leaf Fig (Ficus lyrata) is a popular houseplant known for its large, violin-shaped leaves. It is not a good choice for cats that chew plants, because its leaves and stems contain irritating milky sap.

The sap contains ficin, an enzyme that can irritate the mouth and digestive tract, along with other plant compounds that can bother the skin. When a cat bites a leaf or stem, the sap can cause local burning or stomach upset. Direct sap contact may also lead to redness or itchiness on the skin.

Most cases are mild, but a cat may drool, paw at the mouth, vomit, have diarrhea, lose appetite, or develop skin redness where sap touched. Place fiddle leaf figs where cats truly cannot reach them. If your cat chews the plant or gets sap on its skin, clean the area and contact a veterinarian if symptoms continue or worsen.
name: Fiddle Leaf Fig
safetyNotes: Main hazard: Milky latex sap in the leaves and stems can irritate the mouth, stomach, and skin.
Symptoms: Drooling, mouth pain, vomiting, diarrhea, reduced appetite, or skin redness after sap contact.
Exposure risk: Large leaves can attract curious cats, and repeated nibbling can keep the stomach irritated.
Action: Keep the plant out of reach, rinse sap from skin or fur, and call a vet if vomiting or irritation persists.

symptoms.name: Oral Irritation (Pain and burning sensation in the mouth, tongue, and lips)
symptoms.onset: Immediate (Upon chewing or biting into the leaf/stem).

symptoms.name: Drooling / Hypersalivation
symptoms.onset: Immediate to Acute (Shortly after oral contact).
